items.title: Rear-door hinge corrosion and false latching
items.summary: In salt-belt states corrosion in the rear-door hinges, combined with misaligned latches, could let the doors close in a 'false latch' condition.

items.title: Heater bolt can rupture the fuel pipe
items.summary: Too little clearance between a heater mounting bolt and a fuel delivery pipe (and a rear heater hose clip) could rupture the pipe and leak fuel.

items.title: Oil-cooler hose can melt on the exhaust manifold
items.summary: An improperly installed oil-cooler hose could touch the exhaust manifold and melt.

items.title: Overfilled automatic transmission can spill fluid on the exhaust
items.summary: Overfilled ATF could bleed through an air groove onto the exhaust manifold as the oil warmed up.

items.title: Reese trailer-hitch receiver weld
items.summary: Equipment recall by Reese Products: the weld on the hitch receiver could break.

timeline.change: September: Isuzu announces the Rodeo Bighorn in Japan, a compact 4WD wagon on its pickup chassis
US launch as the Trooper II two-door: 1.95 L gas four (82 hp) or 2.2 L diesel, four-speed manual, rear seat optional
Four-door body, 2.3 L gas four, 2.2 L turbo-diesel (not in California), five-speed, auto-locking hubs and a 21.9 gal tank
Facelift with flush rectangular headlights and a new grille, wider track, P235/75R15 tires and a four-door LS
Optional 2.8 L GM V6; one-year-only short-wheelbase Trooper RS two-door
Recalls for the oil-cooler hose (90V166) and automatic transmission overfill (90V167); NHTSA's owner complaints include under-hood fires and stripped wheel studs
December: replaced by the second-generation Trooper

identify.intro: First-generation Troopers were sold under many names and with engines the US never got, so check what you're looking at, especially with right-hand-drive Japanese or Australian imports.

items.head: Chassis codes by engine
items.body: Wikipedia lists UBS13 (1.95 L G200Z), UBS16 (2.3 L 4ZD1), UBS17 (2.6 L 4ZE1), UBS52 (2.2 L C223 / C223T diesel) and UBS55 (2.8 L 4JB1 diesel). The US V6 trucks use GM's 2.8 L pushrod engine.

items.head: Facelift
items.body: 1984–86 trucks have the original front end; from 1987 the Trooper II has flush rectangular headlights and a new grille.

items.head: Trooper RS
items.body: The 1989-only US short-wheelbase two-door has a wheelbase of about 90 inches instead of 104, a 2.6 L four, 4.77:1 gears and 15 x 7 'snowflake' alloys.

items.head: Re-badges
items.body: Holden Jackaroo (Australia and New Zealand), Isuzu Bighorn and Subaru Bighorn (Japan), Chevrolet Trooper (Indonesia and South America) and Caribe 442 (Venezuela) are the same truck. SsangYong's Korando Family is licence-built with its own bodywork.

items.head: Bighorn Irmscher R
items.body: A limited run of 100 Japanese-market Bighorns with Irmscher graphics, a hood scoop, fender flares, Recaro seats and an Irmscher wheel, all cosmetic, with the 2.8 L intercooled turbo-diesel.

values.intro: First-generation Troopers are still cheap, but tidy, rust-free two-doors and rare diesels are starting to pull ahead.
values.note: Based on 13 Bring a Trailer first-generation sales, October 2024 – July 2026: $3,500 (a 2.6-powered 1986) to $14,250 (a 1986 Trooper II LS two-door five-speed). A 1991 Bighorn Irmscher turbo-diesel sold for $25,000.

paragraphs: Every first-generation Bighorn, Jackaroo and export Trooper is now well past 25 years old, so it can be imported to the US under the 25-year exemption from federal safety and emissions standards. That's the route to the 2.8-liter 4JB1 diesels and the Japanese special editions the US never got. Car and Driver reported that the Irmscher R Bighorn sold in 2019 had arrived in the US in 2015.
Federal eligibility doesn't guarantee registration everywhere, and California is the hardest state for imported diesels, so check your state's titling and emissions rules before you buy.
